The cell cases from the R pages on [cell options (R)](f-cell-options-r.html),
[captions and descriptions (R)](g-captions-r.html), [image formats
(R)](e-image-formats-r.html), [wide and tall figures
(R)](h-wide-and-tall-r.html), and [wide figures in galleries
(R)](i-wide-galleries-r.html), on matplotlib figures. The YAML header sets
`loop`, so the [looping gallery](#sec-looping-gallery) wraps around.

```yaml
---
filters:
  - panzoom
panzoom:
  hint: false
  loop: true
---
```

Jupyter figures are shown at their size in inches × 96 px, and written at twice
that, so a figure here opens at up to twice its size on the page. Quarto gives
each figure that width, so one wider than about 8 inches runs past the column.
The collages here are at most 8 inches wide, where the R pages use 25.

The plots are drawn with these helpers:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def wave(k=1):
    x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 400)
    col = plt.cm.Dark2(k - 1)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
    ax.fill_between(x, np.sin(k * x), color=col, alpha=0.35, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot(x, np.sin(k * x), color=col, linewidth=2)
    ax.set(title=f"Wave {k}", xlabel="x", ylabel="sin(kx)")
    plt.show()


# A collage: `n` panels side by side, like a wide patchwork figure.
def collage(n=12, height=0.8, width=8):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n, figsize=(width, height), layout="constrained")
    for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
        ax.plot(np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=200)), color=plt.cm.viridis(i / n))
        ax.set_title(f"Panel {i + 1}", fontsize=5)
        ax.tick_params(labelsize=4)
    plt.show()


# A tall strip: `n` rows stacked, like a tall patchwork figure.
def strip(seed=2, n=8):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n, 1, figsize=(3, 10), layout="constrained")
    for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
        ax.plot(np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=100)), color=plt.cm.plasma(i / n))
        ax.set_title(f"Strip {seed}, row {i + 1}", fontsize=7)
        ax.tick_params(labelsize=5)
    plt.show()
```

## Looping gallery {#sec-looping-gallery expect-open="panzoom"}

One cell with three plots, joined by `group: waves` under the `panzoom` cell
option. Each opens in panzoom, in a three-image gallery. The YAML header sets
`loop: true` under the `panzoom:` option, so the gallery wraps around: on wave
one, the left arrow key or the previous button goes to wave three, and on wave
three, the right arrow key or the next button goes back to wave one.

```{python}
#| panzoom:
#|   group: waves
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0"
#|   - "A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0"
#|   - "A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0"
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "Wave 1: y = sin(x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is
#|     shaded."
#|   - "Wave 2: y = sin(2x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is
#|     shaded."
#|   - "Wave 3: y = sin(3x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is
#|     shaded."

for k in range(1, 4):
    wave(k)
```

## Text between plots in a group {expect-open="panzoom" expect-steps="true"}

One cell with `group: printed` under the `panzoom` cell option, printing text
between its two plots. Jupyter keeps the outputs in order, so the text sits
between the plots on the page, unlike [`fig-show: hold` in
knitr](f-cell-options-r.html#sec-plots-held-to-the-end-of-a-cell). They open in
panzoom as a two-image gallery, each with its own caption.

```{python}
#| panzoom:
#|   group: printed
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0"
#|   - "A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0"
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "Wave 1: y = sin(x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is
#|     shaded."
#|   - "Wave 2: y = sin(2x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is
#|     shaded."

wave(1)
print("Printed between the two plots.")
wave(2)
```

## Citations {expect-references=""}

A labeled figure with a citation in its caption, and a description with math and

```{python}

```

## Long description {expect-open="panzoom" expect-scroll="description"}

A cell with a description longer than its panel, under the `panzoom` cell
option. It opens in panzoom, and the description panel scrolls. Tab reaches the
panel, and the arrow keys, Page Up and Page Down, Home, End, and Space scroll
it.

```{python}
#| panzoom:
#|   description: >-
#|     This description is long on purpose: it is taller than the space the
#|     viewer gives a description, so its panel scrolls. With a mouse or
#|     trackpad, scrolling over the panel scrolls it. From the keyboard, Tab
#|     moves focus to the panel, and then the arrow keys, Page Up and Page Down,
#|     Home, End and Space scroll it, as they would scroll a page. The image
#|     stays where it is meanwhile, and the page behind the viewer doesn't move.
#|     Tab again moves on to the close button, and Esc still closes the viewer.
#|     Plots like this one often come with long notes: what was measured, how,
#|     and over what range; what the axes mean; what to look for and what to
#|     ignore. Notes like these can run to several paragraphs, and a reader who
#|     uses the keyboard must be able to read all of them, not just the lines
#|     that fit. In a short window, or on a phone, the panel is smaller still,
#|     so even a description of two or three sentences can scroll there. The
#|     panel is a Tab stop only while it scrolls, so a short description adds no
#|     extra stop. The rest of this description only adds length, so that it
#|     scrolls in every window the tests use, including the wide screen, where
#|     the panel is tallest and its lines are longest. The wave rises from zero
#|     to one over the first quarter of each period, falls back to zero at the
#|     half period, reaches minus one at three quarters, and returns to zero at
#|     the end of the period. The shaded area above the axis equals the shaded
#|     area below it over each whole period, so the wave's mean is zero.
#|     Doubling k halves the period and doubles the number of crossings, and the
#|     shading follows the curve wherever it goes. The curve is drawn with 400
#|     points, enough that it looks smooth at any zoom the viewer allows. Its
#|     color comes from the Dark2 palette, one color per wave, and its shading
#|     is the same color at a third of the strength, so the curve stays the
#|     strongest line in the plot. The title names the wave, the x axis runs
#|     over two whole periods, and the y axis is labeled with the formula the
#|     curve follows. Each of these choices is made once, in the helper, so
#|     every wave on this page is drawn the same way and only k changes. Nothing
#|     in this description is needed for the test except its length: a
#|     description this long scrolls in any window.
#| fig-alt: "A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0"
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Wave 1: y = sin(x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is shaded.

wave(1)
```

## png and pdf {expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="contain"}

A plot written as both png and pdf. Jupyter ignores a cell's `fig-format`, so
the cell sets matplotlib's formats itself, and back to the default (retina png)
after. The page shows the png, which opens in panzoom.

```{python}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-alt: "A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0"
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Wave 2: y = sin(2x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is shaded.

%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["png", "pdf"]
wave(2)
%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["retina"]
```

## jpeg {expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="contain"}

A plot written as jpeg, set the same way. It opens in panzoom.

```{python}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-alt: "A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0"
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Wave 3: y = sin(3x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is shaded.

%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["jpeg"]
wave(3)
%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["retina"]
```

## Tall strip {expect-fit="width" shift-scroll="none" alt-scroll="y"}

A 3 × 10 inch strip. It opens at screen width from its top, and Alt+scroll moves
up and down. Shift+scroll doesn't move it.

```{python}
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-alt: "A column of 8 small line plots of random walks"
#| fig-cap: "A 3 × 10 inch strip of 8 random walks."

strip(seed=2)
```

## Fit to width {expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="width" expect-zoom-out="yes"}

An ordinary plot with `fit: width`. Filling the width makes the plot taller than
the screen, so it opens closer than the whole plot and zooms out to it.

```{python}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: width
#| fig-alt: "A sine curve, shaded between the curve and y = 0"
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Wave 4: y = sin(4x); the area between the curve and y = 0 is shaded.

wave(4)
```

## Fit to height on a wide figure {expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="height" expect-zoom-out="yes"}

An 8 × 3 inch figure with `fit: height`. It isn't a strip, since shown whole it
is over a quarter of the screen tall, so `fit: auto` would open it whole. With
`fit: height`, it opens filling the screen height, up to its real size, at the
spot you clicked, and zooms out to the whole figure.

```{python}
#| panzoom:
#|   fit: height
#| fig-alt: "A row of 3 small line plots of random walks, each in its own color"
#| fig-cap: "An 8 × 3 inch collage of 3 random walks."

collage(n=3, height=3)
```

## Gallery of two collages {expect-fit="height"}

Two collages in a gallery, 6.4 × 0.8 inches (12 panels) and 8 × 0.8 inches (15
panels), so their panels have the same shape. Each opens at screen height. The
left and right arrow keys and dragging pan along the collage, and at its end the
next press changes collages, as do the previous and next buttons. Each collage
stops clear of the buttons.

```{python}
#| panzoom:
#|   group: collages
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "A row of 12 small line plots of random walks, each in its own color"
#|   - "A row of 15 small line plots of random walks, each in its own color"
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "A 6.4 × 0.8 inch collage of 12 random walks."
#|   - "An 8 × 0.8 inch collage of 15 random walks."

collage(n=12, width=6.4)
collage(n=15)
```

## Strips side by side {expect-fit="width"}


## Collages in a custom layout {expect-fit="height" expect-steps="true"}

Three collages as subfigures with `layout: [[1, 1], [1]]`: two side by side, and

gallery in reading order.

```{python}

```
